extracted.intended_audience: HIV clinical researchers, pharmacologists, clinical trialists, and grant reviewers designing biomarker-based adherence and PK studies
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating hair (and complementary biological) measures as long-term biomarkers of antiretroviral exposure, adherence, effectiveness, and toxicity within HIV prevention and treatment clinical trials (oral PrEP, vaginal ring, long-acting injectables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Residual dapivirine in used ring as long-term adherence indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: A residual dapivirine level in the used ring of <22 milligrams (mg) served as an indicator of good adherence over a longer period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Residual ring concentrations can vary by site of insertion, method of insertion, ring washing, use of other vaginal products, active menses or intercourse; interpret residual levels in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plasma drug levels as short-term adherence snapshot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plasma drug levels represent only the most recent doses taken and reflect a snapshot of exposure (e.g., short-term adherence ~8 hours use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plasma levels are susceptible to intra-individual day-to-day variability and can be artificially elevated by 'white coat adherence' (taking drug before the visit). Use plasma levels primarily as short-term measure and interpret alongside long-term metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine short- and long-term pharmacologic measures and triangulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining short- and long-term pharmacologic measures (plasma, hair, DBS, residual ring) can provide insight on patterns of adherence (e.g., white coat use, daily dosing, on-demand use, multiweek holidays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a dapivirine plasma level always ≥95 pg/ml with low dapivirine hair suggests ring insertion just prior to visits; consistently high plasma and hair with low ring levels suggests good monthly adherence; high proximal hair and undetectable distal hair suggests a multiweek holiday. Triangulation of measures should be used to model and classify adherence patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: PK monitoring essential for long-acting injectables
rubrics_metrics.description: In any study involving long-acting (LA) agents, adequate exposure to the medication (e.g. drug levels above a certain threshold) must be maintained throughout and at the end of the dosing period; the 'pharmacokinetic tail' must leave a comfortable margin for protective or treatment efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because injectables lack an easy clinical surrogate for exposure (e.g. viral suppression), PK monitoring (plasma and hair) is crucial, particularly to detect missed/delayed injections and end-of-interval exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate PK variability in real-world diverse populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial PK evaluations are often performed in small numbers of 'ideal' patients; PK parameters modeled in early-phase studies can differ significantly in diverse, real-world populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies to examine factors that influence PK variability (e.g., demographics, comorbidities, concomitant medications, body mass) and include PK monitoring in phase 2/3 and implementation studies to inform roll-out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hair as a long-term exposure metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Many drugs are incorporated from the systemic circulation into hair as it grows; hair concentrations serve as long-term measures of exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hair reliably grows in the occipital scalp at ~1 centimeter per month, so distance from the scalp marks time. Hair collection does not require phlebotomy, is stored/shipped at room temperature without biohazard precautions, and has feasibility advantages in resource-limited settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: High acceptability of hair collection when incorporated early
rubrics_metrics.description: When hair collection is incorporated from the beginning of the protocol with field staff and participant education, high rates of acceptability of hair collection (>95%) have been documented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include participant education, pictures/videos for various hair styles, and trained field staff to achieve high consent/collection rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hair collection procedure (field protocol)
rubrics_metrics.description: A standardized 8-step hair collection procedure: 1) Clean scissors blades with alcohol and dry; 2) Lift top layer of hair from occipital region and isolate a small thatch (50–100 strands) from underneath; 3) Cut as close to the scalp as possible; 4) Place thatch inside an unfolded piece of foil; 5) Place a narrow label over the distal end to denote directionality if strands long enough; 6) Refold foil to enclose sample; 7) Place study ID on folded foil; 8) Place foil inside plastic bag with desiccant and seal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide pictures and videos for various hair styles (short, cropped, curly, weaves, braids). Samples kept at room temperature prior to batch shipment without biohazard precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory hair sample processing protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: For analysis, the proximal section of the thatch (~1–2 cm depending on exposure window) is cut, chopped to 1–2 mm length segments; 5 mg is weighed and processed with extraction and LC-MS/MS analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For TFV/FTC: extract with 50% methanol/water containing 1% trifluoroacetic acid, 0.5% hydrazine dihydrochloride and internal standard in a 37°C shaking water bath overnight (>12 hours) prior to LC-MS/MS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic assay validation and QA metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assays for measuring TFV and FTC in hair validated and DAIDS CPQA-approved with method ranges and performance characteristics: TFV validated from 0.002 ng/mg to 0.400 ng/mg hair; FTC validated from 0.02 to 4.0 ng/mg; relative error (%) and precision (coefficients of variation) for spiked QC hair samples at low, medium and high concentrations are all <15%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use validated assays and QA programs (e.g., DAIDS CPQA) for acceptance; report detection limits and include QC performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of sampling strategy for assay testing (cost-efficient case-control sampling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure hair levels for every visit from all seroconverters and from a simple random sample of controls who did not acquire HIV, using ≈3 controls per case (3:1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random sampling of a small fraction of non-seroconverters provides nearly as much information as testing all specimens but is more cost-efficient. Use sampling fraction weights to combine data from seroconverters (sampled with certainty) and sampled controls to obtain estimates for the entire study population (software examples: svyset/svy: in Stata; SurveyReg/SurveyLogistic in SAS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis approach for associating hair levels with seroconversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fit a discrete-time Cox model using the pooled logistic regression approach to estimate the association of hair TFV and FTC levels with seroconversion, controlling for covariates associated with incidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine hair levels as categorical (e.g., quartiles) and continuous (log-transformed), compare explanatory utility of plasma and self-report, and use survey-weighting to account for sampling fractions. Log-transformed hair levels often predict outcomes better and more closely meet linearity assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and power planning exemplar
rubrics_metrics.description: With assumptions in SEARCH PrEP, expect ~100 HIV seroconversions among persons on PrEP; analyzing 100 cases and 300 controls (400 × 13 visits = 5200 samples) provides high cost-efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power example: comparing bottom quartile vs top three quartiles, power ≥80% for an odds ratio ≥2.1. Multiple observations per person and inclusion of additional sampled participants (e.g., for toxicity) improve power and precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hair levels as predictors of renal toxicity and sampling for toxicity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess association of hair levels with renal toxicity using samples measured for effectiveness and supplemented with up to 100 persons who reach eCrCl ≤60 ml/min or whose CrCl declines by >15% (100 × 13 visits = 1300 person-visits); include eGFR-based definitions as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistical methods: use linear mixed effects models to estimate mean percent change in eCrCl from baseline adjusted for covariates; use multivariate logistic regression to assess predictors of renal decline; analyses will account for sampling fractions and certain sampling of seroconverters and toxicity cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling undetectable hair concentrations and transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Because detection limits for TFV and FTC in hair are low, treat undetectable levels as equal to the detection limit. Add the detection limit to all values before log-transformation to reduce influence of small differences between very low hair levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use log-transformed hair levels where appropriate; document censoring and imputation approach for left-censored data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correlations and concordance/discordance to infer adherence patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine scatterplots and Spearman correlation coefficients between hair and plasma concentrations and self-reported adherence, and assess concordance/discordance to infer patterns (e.g., detectable hair despite undetectable plasma suggests intermittent use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model patterns of delayed initiation, frequently missed doses, multiweek holidays, and on-demand use if objective adherence measures are collected and triangulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: DBS and PBMCs relevance limitation by ARV class
rubrics_metrics.description: For medications phosphorylated and trapped intracellularly (e.g., TFV/FTC), intracellular anabolite concentrations in PBMCs or DBS relay information on longer dosing periods. However, INSTIs (e.g., cabotegravir) and NNRTIs (e.g., dapivirine) do not exhibit intracellular phosphorylation, so measurement in DBS does not offer additional advantage to plasma levels for these ARVs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select biological matrix based on ARV pharmacology; note that plasma, PBMCs, DBS, and urine require cold chain and biohazard precautions unlike hair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility/logistics advantage of hair sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Hair collection does not require phlebotomy, is stored and shipped at room temperature without biohazardous precautions, and is therefore feasible and logistically advantageous in resource-limited settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage room-temperature storage and simple field collection to enable large-scale monitoring; provide field materials (foil, labels, desiccants, instructions) and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend hair measures to novel ARV delivery modalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose to 'extend' hair levels to novel modalities of antiretroviral delivery (vaginal rings and injectables) to assess adherence and pharmacokinetics for the first time in these contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For injectables (e.g., LA cabotegravir), examine hair levels (and combination with plasma) for PK monitoring, including end-of-dosing-interval exposure; plan studies to define hair-based PK metrics relevant to protection.
